The advance is still up, but it is working noticeably harder for every point. Each session the buyers push, and each session they keep less of it. Three white soldiers are three full bodies. An advance block is three bodies running out of fuel. Only after an advance, which is the whole difference from the soldiers. Look for it late in a run, far above the averages, where tired buying is the first sign of a top. A fourth bar that closes below the third bar's low confirms the stall turned into a reversal. A fourth green bar with a full body cancels it. The block was a pause, not a top. Shrinking green bodies on a leader are a reason to stop adding and to tighten. The desk does not short an advance block. It stops buying it.

lesson_text: A long red body that opened at its high and fell all session. No wick above, close near the low. After an advance, the stock opened at the top and never saw a higher print. Buyers who had been driving the move were absent from the first minute, and sellers had the whole session to themselves. After an advance, most telling when it comes from a stretched position: far above the averages, after a run of up days, or on a gap up that immediately reversed. A next session that fails to recover the belt hold's midpoint and closes lower confirms it. A close back above the belt hold's open cancels it. The sellers were absorbed and the advance resumes. In a leader, a bearish belt hold on heavy volume is a change of character. The open of that bar is the level. Until the stock reclaims it, assume the easy part of the move is over.

lesson_text: Open and close together at the top of the bar with a long tail below and almost nothing above. A hammer with no body at all. The session sold off and every bit of it was bought back, to the penny. Sellers had the morning and buyers had the afternoon, and the buyers won the argument so completely that the close landed on the open. At the bottom of a pullback or a decline, into a level: a prior low, a rising average, the floor of a range. Its meaning flips with the trend. After an advance a dragonfly is a warning that sellers could reach that far down at all. After a decline, a next session that opens above the doji's close or closes above its high confirms the buyers. After an advance, a close below the tail confirms the sellers. The exact same bar printed after an advance is a hanging man, and the prior trend is the only thing that separates the two names. Look for it where a pullback meets a level that matters: a prior low, a rising average, the bottom of a base. A hammer in the middle of nowhere is just a bar. The next session has to agree. It marks the price where buyers proved they exist. Mark the low of that tail, then let the next bar tell you whether the higher low is real.

lesson_text: A hammer's exact shape: small body near the top, long tail below, almost no wick above. The difference is where it printed. After an advance, sellers were able to press the stock well below the open in the middle of the session. Buyers rescued the close, but the fact that the rescue was needed is the news. Inside an uptrend nobody should have been able to push it that far down. Only after an advance, and ideally after a stretched one: far above the rising averages, several up days in a row, a gap higher that morning. That is where a long tail under the body means the floor just creaked. This name needs confirmation more than almost any other. A next session that opens below the hanging man's body, or a red bar that closes under its low, confirms that the sellers who showed up mid-session came back. A close above the hanging man's high cancels it. The dip was absorbed, and the advance continues as if nothing happened. In a leader that has run, a hanging man is a reason to tighten, not a reason to short. Note the low of the tail. If the stock closes under it, the trade has told you what it thinks.

The downside break pulled in sellers and shook out weak holders, and the close above the inside bar's high says they were all wrong. This is the state a hikkake trader acts on. The best ones form in a leader's tight pullback, where the inside bar is the coil and the false break is the shakeout. The close above the inside bar's high is the confirmation. That is what the name means. A close back below the false break's low cancels it. This is a shakeout with a receipt. The desk reads the false break's low as the stop and the inside bar's high as the trigger that just fired.

lesson_text: A shooting star's shape: small body near the bottom, long wick above, almost nothing below. After a decline, buyers finally managed a real push off the lows during the session. They could not hold it into the close, so the wick is all that remains of the attempt. That attempt is the information: for the first time in a while, someone bought with force. Only after a decline, near a level where the decline could end: a prior low, a base bottom, a rising average on a bigger timeframe. lesson_text: Open and close nearly level, sitting in the middle of a bar with long wicks both ways. A wide, genuinely two-sided fight that ended where it began. Buyers won part of the session, sellers won part of it, and neither side could keep anything by the close. At the end of a strong move in either direction, where the first real disagreement shows up. It also appears in the middle of ranges, where it means little. The next session picks a side. A close beyond the doji's high or low, in either direction, is the resolution the doji was waiting for. Another doji or a small inside bar keeps the question open. Nothing is cancelled, but nothing is decided either. A long-legged doji after a straight run is the market pausing to think. The desk does not act on the doji. It acts on the bar that resolves it, in whichever direction it resolves.

Size is measured against this stock's own recent bodies, so the bar means the same thing on a cheap stock and an expensive one. Out of a base or through a prior high it is a breakout bar. The first long white bar after a quiet stretch is usually the one worth noticing. The next session holds the top half of the bar. Heavy volume on the bar itself makes it worth more. A close back below the long white bar's low cancels it. The buying was retraced. The desk reads a long white bar on big volume as institutional buying, which is the only kind that lasts. The bar's low is the level. Above it, the buyers are winning.

lesson_text: A small body near the bottom of the bar with a long spike above it, at least twice the body. Little or no tail below. After an advance, buyers pushed to a new high during the session and sellers took every bit of that gain back by the close. The spike is the ground the buyers could not hold. The close near the low says who won the day. Only after an advance. The identical bar after a decline is an inverted hammer. Look for it at resistance: a prior high, the top of a range, a round number the stock has stalled at before, or a stock that is stretched far above its averages. A next session that opens below the star's body, or closes below its low, confirms the rejection. A gap down is the loudest version. A close above the star's high cancels it. The buyers came back and took the ground the spike had lost. The high of the spike is the line. If a leader prints a shooting star into a level and then closes back above the spike within a session or two, the rejection failed and that is bullish information. If it cannot, the spike was the top for now.

lesson_text: Three straight red bars, each opening inside the previous body and each closing near its low. Steady, orderly distribution. No panic, no gap, just three sessions in a row where sellers finished the day in control. Each bar opens a little higher than the last close, offers a brief hope, and then sells off into the close. Only after an advance, especially a mature one. Three red bars at the start of a decline mean something. Three red bars three weeks into a decline are just the trend. The third bar is the pattern. A fourth bar that cannot reclaim the third bar's open confirms it. A close back above the first crow's open cancels it. The whole sequence was retraced. Three closes near the lows in a row is a leader telling you the buyers have stepped aside. The desk reads it as a trend change in progress, not a dip to buy.

Three soldiers off a base low are the picture of a bottom being built. The same three bars at the end of a long run are an advance block or deliberation, and the catalog names them differently. The third bar is the pattern. A fourth bar that holds above the third bar's open confirms it. A close back below the first soldier's open cancels it. The desk likes soldiers out of a base on rising volume. The low of the first soldier is the stop most of the room would use, and the sequence is the kind of start a leader makes.

lesson_text: Three dojis in a row. Three consecutive sessions that could not settle on a direction. Unusual enough to be worth a look, because markets rarely stay undecided that long without something happening next. No trend is required for the name. At the end of a long move in either direction it is the clearest pause the catalog has. In the middle of a dead range it means the range is dead. The first bar that closes outside the three-doji range picks the direction. Nothing to cancel. It resolves one way or the other. Three dojis after a run is a coiled spring. The desk does not guess the direction. It trades the break, in whichever direction the break comes.

lesson_text: Long lower tail, small body near the high: the hammer and hanging man geometry. The session sold off and was bought back. That much is true in any context. What is missing is the trend that would tell you whether this is a hammer at a low or a hanging man at a high. The chart before it is flat or unreadable, so the catalog prints the shape and refuses to guess. You will see it in choppy ranges and quiet tapes where there is no clear trend to lean on. It is still worth a look when the tail touches a level: a range floor, a prior close, a moving average. The same test as a hammer: an open above the body or a close above the high says buyers followed through. A close below the tail's low says the buying was not real. An umbrella in a range is a level, not a signal. Note where the tail bottomed and watch whether the range respects it. The name will change to hammer or hanging man once the chart gives it a trend.
